topics.name: Bernoulli’s principle
topics.kicker: Faster flow means lower pressure · A key idea behind airplane lift
topics.briefing: Bernoulli’s principle says that when a fluid such as air or water speeds up, its pressure drops. The Swiss scientist Daniel Bernoulli published the idea in his 1738 book _Hydrodynamica_. It helps explain how airplane wings get lift, how perfume sprayers pull up liquid, and why a ping-pong ball can float in the stream from a hair dryer.
topics.answerHtml: Bernoulli’s principle (accept Bernoulli’s equation, Bernoulli’s law, or Bernoulli effect; prompt on Bernoulli; do not accept “Venturi effect”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The 1738 book that introduced this principle, _Hydrodynamica_, also argued that a gas pushes on its container because countless tiny particles keep hitting the walls, an early version of the kinetic theory of gases. That book’s author came from a famous family of mathematicians.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle stating that a fluid’s pressure drops as its speed increases.

tossups.p: Leonhard Euler [“OY-ler”] wrote this principle’s equation in its modern form, which applies along a streamline in a steady, incompressible flow with no viscosity. That equation says pressure plus one-half density times speed squared plus density times g times height stays constant.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rule of fluid dynamics, which says that faster-moving fluids have lower pressure.

tossups.p: This principle’s namesake had a bitter rivalry with his own father, Johann, who wrote a competing book called _Hydraulica_ and dated it earlier than his son’s. The son’s book, _Hydrodynamica_, came out in 1738.
tossups.r: It helps explain airplane lift. For 10 points, name this principle stating that when a fluid flows faster, its pressure falls.

tossups.p: The “equal transit time” fallacy, a popular but wrong explanation of lift that uses this principle, claims that air flowing over the top of an airfoil must meet the air from below at the back edge. In reality, the air over the top arrives first.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle of fluids, which helps explain airplane lift by linking faster flow to lower pressure.

tossups.p: In the 1730s, Henri Pitot [“PEE-toh”] invented a tube to measure the speed of river water. Airplanes use such tubes, along with this principle, to find their airspeed by comparing the pressure of air rammed to a stop in the tube with that of the air flowing past.
tossups.r: Perfume sprayers also rely on it. For 10 points, name this principle stating that faster-moving fluids exert less pressure.

tossups.p: A law named for Evangelista Torricelli [“tor-ih-CHEL-ee”] says that water leaks from a hole in a tank at the speed it would reach falling from the water’s surface, and it can be derived from this principle. This principle is really conservation of energy for a moving fluid.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle stating that a fluid’s pressure drops when its speed increases.

tossups.p: A Venturi meter uses this principle to find a liquid’s speed by comparing the pressure in a wide part of a pipe with that in a narrow throat, where the liquid moves faster. A carburetor uses the same effect to pull fuel into a stream of air.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle, published in 1738, which says that faster fluids have lower pressure.

tossups.p: A 1911 collision between the warship HMS _Hawke_ and the ocean liner _Olympic_, sister ship of the _Titanic_, was blamed on suction explained by this principle. Two ships sailing close together can be pulled toward each other for the same reason.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle stating that fast-moving fluids, like the water squeezed between the ships, have lower pressure.

tossups.p: Engineers often write this principle in terms of “head,” saying that pressure head, velocity head, and elevation head add up to a constant total for an ideal fluid. The principle holds exactly only for a fluid with no viscosity that cannot be compressed.
tossups.r: Perfume atomizers use it to draw liquid up a thin tube. For 10 points, name this principle linking faster fluid speed to lower pressure.

tossups.p: A water aspirator in a chemistry lab uses this principle, pulling air out of a flask with a fast jet of water. Race cars carry upside-down wings so that this principle presses them onto the track, a push called downforce.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle that explains how airplane wings get lift, because faster-moving air has lower pressure.

tossups.p: This principle is often used with the continuity equation, which says that a fluid in a pipe speeds up wherever the pipe gets narrower, since area times speed stays the same. Blowing between two empty soda cans makes them roll toward each other because of this principle.
tossups.r: It helps explain how airplanes fly. For 10 points, name this principle that says faster-moving fluids exert less pressure.

tossups.p: Blowing hard through an upside-down funnel can hold a ping-pong ball inside instead of pushing it out, and a ping-pong ball can hover in the stream of a hair dryer; both tricks are classroom demonstrations of this principle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle of fluid flow, published by a Swiss scientist in 1738, which helps explain airplane lift.

tossups.p: In this principle’s equation, one-half times density times speed squared is called dynamic pressure; adding it to the static pressure gives the total, or stagnation, pressure. Because of this principle, strong hurricane winds racing over a roof can help lift it off a house.
tossups.r: Wind blowing across a chimney top helps draw smoke up for the same reason. For 10 points, name this principle linking faster fluid flow to lower pressure.

tossups.p: In a Bunsen burner, gas rushing out of a narrow jet pulls air in through holes near the bottom of the barrel, thanks to this principle. Many airbrushes use a fast stream of air to pull paint up from a cup in a similar way.
tossups.r: This principle is named for a Swiss scientist. For 10 points, name this principle stating that faster-moving fluids have lower pressure.

tossups.p: This principle’s namesake, who trained as a doctor, later used mathematics to argue that inoculating people against smallpox would save lives. He described this principle in his 1738 book _Hydrodynamica_, and his father and uncle were also famous mathematicians.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle, which says that when a fluid speeds up, its pressure drops.

trap.title: Not Pascal or Venturi
trap.body: Several fluid answer lines sound alike. Pascal’s principle says pressure applied to a trapped fluid spreads equally in all directions, as in hydraulic lifts, and Archimedes’ principle is about buoyancy and floating. The Venturi effect is a special case of this principle in a narrowing pipe, and the Magnus effect is what curves a spinning ball, so real answer lines may refuse those names.
trap.fix: Speed and pressure trading off, wings, sprayers, Pitot tubes, or _Hydrodynamica_ mean this principle. Hydraulic jacks and brakes mean Pascal; floating and displaced water mean Archimedes; a spinning, curving ball means the Magnus effect; and saying just “Bernoulli” earns only a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Bernoulli’s principle (accept Bernoulli’s equation, Bernoulli’s law, or Bernoulli effect; prompt on Bernoulli; do not accept “Venturi effect”)

topics.name: Hall effect
topics.kicker: Sideways voltage from a magnet · Used to sense magnetic fields
topics.briefing: In 1879, a graduate student named Edwin Hall discovered that when an electric current flows through a thin metal strip inside a magnetic field, a small voltage appears across the strip, sideways to the current. The magnetic force pushes the moving charges toward one edge, and that pile-up creates the voltage. Tiny Hall effect sensors detect magnets in phones, cars, and electric motors.
topics.answerHtml: Hall effect (accept specific types such as the quantum Hall effect; prompt on Hall voltage or Hall alone)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1980, Klaus von Klitzing found that in a very thin, very cold layer of electrons, the resistance tied to this effect comes only in values equal to Planck’s constant over the electron’s charge squared, divided by a whole number. He won the 1985 Nobel Prize in Physics.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect in which a magnetic field produces a voltage across a conductor, sideways to the current.

tossups.p: Daniel Tsui and Horst Störmer [“SHTUR-mer”] discovered a “fractional” version of this effect in 1982, which Robert Laughlin explained using strange quasiparticles that carry one-third of an electron’s charge. All three shared the 1998 Nobel Prize in Physics.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, discovered in 1879, in which a sideways voltage appears across a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.

tossups.p: While a graduate student at Johns Hopkins under Henry Rowland, this effect’s discoverer tested a claim in James Clerk Maxwell’s _Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism_ that a magnet pushes on a wire carrying a current, not on the current itself.
tossups.r: In 1879, he found a tiny voltage across a thin metal strip. For 10 points, name this effect named for that American physicist.

tossups.p: This effect’s namesake coefficient equals one divided by the number of charge carriers per unit volume times their charge, so measuring it tells scientists how many free electrons a metal has. The voltage it produces is larger in a thinner sample.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect in which a magnetic field pushes moving charges to one side of a conductor, creating a voltage.

tossups.p: In some semiconductors, the voltage from this effect points the opposite way from what electrons would produce, showing that the current is carried by positive “holes.” Scientists use this effect to tell n-type semiconductors from p-type ones, and it is much stronger in semiconductors than in metals.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, discovered in 1879, in which a sideways voltage appears across a current-carrying strip in a magnetic field.

tossups.p: SpaceX’s Starlink satellites adjust their orbits with small electric engines named for this effect, which use a magnetic field to trap swirling electrons and an electric field to fire out charged gas. The European probe SMART-1 used one of those engines to reach the Moon in 2004.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect in which a magnetic field creates a sideways voltage in a conductor carrying a current.

tossups.p: Brushless electric motors use tiny sensors based on this effect to track the position of their spinning magnets, and cars use similar sensors to measure wheel speed for anti-lock brakes. Some phones and tablets use them to notice when a magnetic cover is closed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, the sideways voltage produced across a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.

tossups.p: National laboratories use a quantized version of this effect as their standard for electrical resistance, and since 2019 the constant h over e squared, about 25,813 ohms, has had an exact value. That constant is named for Klaus von Klitzing.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect in which charges pushed sideways by a magnetic field build up a voltage across a conductor.

tossups.p: The voltage from this effect equals the current times the magnetic field, divided by the product of three things: the density of charge carriers, their charge, and the sample’s thickness. Reversing the magnetic field flips the sign of the voltage this effect produces.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect discovered by an American physicist in 1879, in which a magnetic field makes a sideways voltage across a current.

tossups.p: This effect was discovered in 1879, eighteen years before J. J. Thomson discovered the electron, so its discoverer did not yet know what was actually flowing in a wire. Its voltage is proportional to both the current and the strength of the magnetic field.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect in which a magnetic field pushes moving charges sideways, building up a voltage across a conductor.

tossups.p: When this effect reaches a steady state, the sideways electric force on each moving charge exactly cancels the magnetic part of the Lorentz force, so the charges’ drift speed equals the electric field divided by the magnetic field.
tossups.r: The right-hand rule tells which edge of the conductor the charges pile up on. For 10 points, name this effect, in which a magnetic field creates a sideways voltage.

tossups.p: Teslameters, also called gaussmeters, usually measure the strength of a magnetic field with a small probe based on this effect. Clamp meters that measure direct current in a wire without touching it often rely on the same effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, discovered in 1879, in which a voltage appears across a current-carrying strip placed in a magnetic field.

tossups.p: Measurements of this effect, together with resistance, tell chip makers how easily charges move through a semiconductor, a property called mobility. In copper, the direction of the voltage from this effect shows that the charges carrying the current are negative.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which a magnetic field produces a voltage across a conductor at right angles to the current.

tossups.p: Some gaming keyboards and joysticks use magnet sensors based on this effect, which have no touching parts to wear out. Many car engines use the same kind of sensor to track the position of the crankshaft.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, the sideways voltage that appears across a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.

tossups.p: This effect’s American discoverer went on to teach physics at Harvard for many years. He had found this effect while working toward his doctorate at Johns Hopkins University. In this effect, the magnetic field, the current, and the voltage all point at right angles to one another.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, discovered in 1879, that produces a sideways voltage in a conductor sitting in a magnetic field.

clues.t: A voltage appears across a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, at right angles to the current
Discovered in 1879 by its American namesake, a graduate student at Johns Hopkins University
Tiny sensors based on it detect magnets in phones, cars, and electric motors
The magnetic force pushes moving charges toward one edge, and the pile-up of charge makes the voltage
In steady state, the sideways electric force balances the magnetic part of the Lorentz force, so drift speed equals E divided by B
Its namesake coefficient equals 1 divided by (carrier density times charge), revealing how many charge carriers a material has
The direction of its voltage reveals the sign of the charge carriers, showing positive “holes” in p-type semiconductors
Much stronger in semiconductors than in metals, which have far more free electrons; thinner samples give bigger voltages
Its voltage is proportional to both the current and the magnetic field strength; reversing the field flips the voltage
Probes based on it measure magnetic field strength in teslameters, also called gaussmeters
Brushless motors use its sensors to track their magnets; cars use them for wheel speed and crankshaft position
The right-hand rule tells which edge of the conductor the charges pile up on
Klaus von Klitzing found its “quantum” version in 1980: the resistance equals h over e squared divided by a whole number (1985 Nobel Prize)
Daniel Tsui and Horst Störmer found a “fractional” version (1982); Robert Laughlin explained it with one-third-charge quasiparticles (1998 Nobel Prize)
Labs use its quantized version as the standard for resistance; since 2019, the von Klitzing constant, about 25,813 ohms, is exact
Working under Henry Rowland, its discoverer tested Maxwell’s claim in the _Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism_ that a magnet pushes on a wire, not on the current
Electric spacecraft engines named for it move SpaceX’s Starlink satellites; one carried Europe’s SMART-1 probe to the Moon in 2004
Its voltage equals current times magnetic field, divided by the product of carrier density, carrier charge, and sample thickness
In copper, the direction of its voltage shows that the charges carrying the current are negative
Measured together with resistance, it tells chip makers the mobility of charges in a semiconductor
Clamp meters that measure direct current without touching a wire often rely on it
Some gaming keyboards and joysticks use sensors based on it, which have no touching parts to wear out
Discovered 18 years before J. J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897
Its discoverer later taught physics at Harvard for many years

trap.title: The effect, not its parts
trap.body: Tossups on this effect are full of its ingredients, so players blurt the wrong piece. The Lorentz force is the magnetic push on moving charges that causes the effect, the “Hall voltage” is only its result, and saying just “Hall” names a person. Other magnetic effects, like the Zeeman effect (split spectral lines) or magnetoresistance (resistance changing in a magnetic field), have their own answer lines.
trap.fix: A current, a magnetic field, and a voltage across the conductor, all at right angles, mean this effect, so say the full name, “Hall effect.” Split spectral lines mean the Zeeman effect, and light knocking electrons out of a metal means the photoelectric effect.
trap.line: Real answer line: Hall effect (accept specific types such as the quantum Hall effect; prompt on Hall voltage or Hall alone)

topics.name: Niels Bohr
topics.kicker: Danish father of the quantum atom · Electrons in fixed orbits
topics.briefing: Niels Bohr was a Danish physicist who, in 1913, pictured the atom as a tiny solar system in which electrons can travel only in certain fixed orbits, jumping between them by giving off or absorbing light. That idea explained the colors of light that glowing hydrogen gives off and helped win him the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics. His institute in Copenhagen became a world center for the new science of quantum mechanics.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: When this scientist received the Order of the Elephant in 1947, he chose a coat of arms showing the yin-yang symbol and the Latin motto “Contraria sunt complementa,” or “opposites are complementary.” That motto reflected his principle of complementarity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Danish physicist whose 1913 model of the atom placed electrons in fixed orbits.

tossups.p: This scientist’s theory of the periodic table predicted that element 72 would resemble zirconium rather than the rare earths, and in 1923 two researchers at his institute found it and named it hafnium, after the Latin name for his home city.
tossups.r: Element 107 is also named for him. For 10 points, name this Danish physicist who proposed a model of the hydrogen atom in 1913.

tossups.p: In 1940, as German troops occupied Copenhagen, George de Hevesy [“HEV-eh-shee”] dissolved the gold Nobel Prize medals of Max von Laue and James Franck in aqua regia at this scientist’s institute to hide them from the Nazis. The gold was later recovered and the medals were recast.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Danish physicist who won the 1922 Nobel Prize for his model of the atom.

tossups.p: In 1943, this scientist escaped from occupied Denmark to Sweden on a fishing boat, then flew to Britain in the bomb bay of a Mosquito airplane and passed out from lack of oxygen. He later advised the Manhattan Project under the false name “Nicholas Baker.”
tossups.r: His son Aage later won a Nobel Prize too. For 10 points, name this Danish physicist who modeled the atom with electrons in fixed orbits.

tossups.p: In 1939, this scientist and John Wheeler explained nuclear fission with a liquid-drop model of the nucleus, and he realized that the rare isotope uranium-235 is the one that splits when hit by slow neutrons. Earlier that year, he had carried news of fission’s discovery to the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Danish physicist whose 1913 atomic model put electrons in fixed energy levels.

tossups.p: At a 1927 conference in Como, Italy, this scientist introduced complementarity, the idea that light and electrons show wave or particle behavior depending on the experiment, but never both at once. He and Werner Heisenberg developed the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Danish physicist who won the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on atomic structure.

tossups.p: This scientist’s correspondence principle says that quantum physics must give the same answers as classical physics for very large quantum numbers, such as electrons in huge orbits. In his model, an electron’s angular momentum must be a whole-number multiple of Planck’s constant divided by two pi.
tossups.r: That model explained the lines in hydrogen’s spectrum. For 10 points, name this Danish physicist who proposed it in 1913.

tossups.p: At the 1930 Solvay Conference, this scientist answered Albert Einstein’s “photon box” challenge to quantum mechanics by using Einstein’s own general relativity. This scientist also replied to a famous 1935 paper by Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Danish physicist whose 1913 model of the atom had electrons jumping between fixed orbits.

tossups.p: After working with Ernest Rutherford in Manchester, this scientist published a three-part paper in 1913, often called his “trilogy,” in the journal _Philosophical Magazine_. That work explained the Balmer series of visible lines in hydrogen’s spectrum and the value of the Rydberg constant.
tossups.r: In his model, electrons give off light when they jump down between fixed orbits. For 10 points, name this Danish physicist.

tossups.p: Michael Frayn’s 1998 play _Copenhagen_ imagines what this scientist and his former assistant Werner Heisenberg said during a mysterious 1941 meeting in German-occupied Denmark. The play’s third character is this scientist’s wife, Margrethe.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Danish physicist who won the 1922 Nobel Prize for his work on the structure of atoms.

tossups.p: This scientist’s son Aage won the 1975 Nobel Prize in Physics for work on the structure of atomic nuclei, and his father, Christian, found that carbon dioxide helps blood release oxygen. His brother Harald was a mathematician who won an Olympic silver medal in soccer.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Danish physicist whose model of the atom had electrons in fixed orbits.

tossups.p: The radius of the smallest electron orbit in this scientist’s model of hydrogen, about 0.053 nanometers, is named for him. Arnold Sommerfeld later improved this scientist’s model by allowing electrons to follow elliptical orbits.
tossups.r: His model could not explain atoms with more than one electron, such as helium. For 10 points, name this Danish physicist who proposed that model in 1913.

tossups.p: In 1944, this scientist urged Winston Churchill and Franklin Roosevelt to tell the Soviet Union about the atomic bomb project to avoid an arms race, and in 1950 he wrote an open letter to the United Nations calling for an “open world.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Danish physicist whose model of the atom had electrons jumping between fixed orbits.

tossups.p: In 1921, this scientist opened an institute for theoretical physics at the University of Copenhagen, where young physicists like Werner Heisenberg and Wolfgang Pauli came to work. The institute was later renamed for him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Danish physicist whose 1913 model of the hydrogen atom placed electrons in fixed orbits.

tossups.p: This scientist’s Nobel Prize in Physics was announced at the same time as Albert Einstein’s delayed prize for 1921. This scientist had earlier worked with J. J. Thomson at Cambridge before moving to Manchester to work with Ernest Rutherford.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Danish physicist whose atomic model placed electrons in fixed, numbered energy levels.

trap.title: Not Rutherford or Heisenberg
trap.body: Several founders of atomic physics show up in the same tossups. Ernest Rutherford discovered the nucleus with his gold foil experiment, and this man then put the electrons into fixed orbits around it; Werner Heisenberg, his younger colleague, created matrix mechanics and the uncertainty principle. The family is a trap too: his son Aage won a Nobel Prize in 1975, and his father Christian’s name is on the Bohr effect in blood.
trap.fix: Fixed orbits, energy levels, hydrogen’s spectrum, complementarity, Copenhagen, or element 107 mean this man. The gold foil experiment and the nucleus mean Rutherford; matrix mechanics and uncertainty mean Heisenberg; and a 1975 Nobel for work on atomic nuclei means his son Aage, so give the full name if you can.
trap.line: Real answer line: Niels Bohr (accept Bohr; do not accept “Aage Bohr”)
